source.title: Towards Structured Dynamic Sparse Pre-Training of BERT
source.authors: A. Dietrich; Frithjof Gressmann; Douglas Orr; Ivan Chelombiev; Daniel Justus; C. Luschi

record.tranche_reason: The study compares validation MLM loss across BERT-family models at different FLOPs, which bears on scaling of pretraining loss, but it does not fit or evaluate a power law.
record.gate_note: The study reports loss-versus-FLOPs curves for dense, static-sparse and dynamic-sparse BERT models. These results bear on V1's scaling behavior, but the plotted values do not establish whether the loss follows a power law. Results about sparse-training efficiency, block-size choices and learning-rate scaling do not test the other claim versions.
record.test_reason: This is a sparse-training efficiency study. It cites Kaplan et al. only as motivation and for a learning-rate rule. The dense BERT-family curve (Tiny to Base, about two orders of FLOPs) serves only as a Pareto baseline for its own DynSparse method. Loss falling with size is shown only in a figure, with no power-law fit or form assessed, and no extrapolation, allocation, shape, transfer or downstream result. Its results do not bear on whether any version holds.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that DynSparse pretraining of BERT is more FLOP-efficient than dense and static-sparse baselines, and remains Pareto-efficient with block sparsity. Experiments cover MLM pretraining at sequence length 128 only.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates dynamic sparse BERT pretraining and FLOP efficiency rather than fitting scaling laws or selecting compute-optimal parameter and token allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: The study reports that sparse-model learning rates differ from dense-model learning rates, and that block-pruning metric and sparsity-update settings affect task performance; these are not tests of the claim's loss-scaling laws.

fits_no_version.finding: The optimal learning rate scales as a power of trainable parameters: log(η) ≈ -0.44 log N for dense and -0.84 log N for sparse models. Kaplan et al.'s log-linear learning-rate rule fit qualitatively worse.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimal learning rate follows a power law in parameter count, with a different exponent for sparse and dense models.

fits_no_version.finding: At matched FLOPs, DynSparse BERT reaches lower MLM loss than the interpolated dense family. It needs 0.48× the FLOPs for BERT-Base-level loss (Fig. 3, Table 1). Static sparsity roughly matches the dense curve.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The loss-versus-compute frontier depends on the training algorithm (dynamic sparsity shifts it), not on compute alone.

record.problems: The claim-relevant results are plotted without numerical loss values in the text, and the study does not fit or evaluate a power-law model. Experiments are limited to BERT MLM pretraining with sequence length 128.
record.rows_left_out: Learning-rate sweeps, block-sparsity comparisons, and sparse-training hyperparameter results were omitted because they do not test the claim versions; see Figures 5–13 and Tables 1, A.2–A.16.

untested.parts: No power-law fit or exponents. No token-count scaling. Dense curve covers about two orders of FLOPs, shown only in a figure.
not tested; no downstream fine-tuning results

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' is wrong. Having loss-versus-FLOPs curves without a fit or a claim about the functional form does not test V1. The paper's only engagement with Kaplan et al. concerns the learning-rate rule, which is not a claim version.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not fit or test a power-law form, report exponents, test token-count scaling, or establish behavior over several orders of magnitude.
